l: The Amores, or Amours
s: anxious lover follows mistress (over any distance and difficult terrain)
q: send the fair _far_ away, _and_ the lover will boldly follow her, without a limit _to his endurance_.

s: anxious lover keeps watch on rival (as though upon an enemy)

l: The Amores, or Amours
s: anxious lover lays siege to mistress (at her threshold when she is obdurate)
q: The one lays siege to stubborn cities, the other to the threshold of his obdurate mistress: the one bursts open gates, and the other, doors.

s: mistress requires gifts and presents (as a return for love)

l: The Amores, or Amours

q: Still, she curses the tyranny of the avaricious procurer; [154] and she does by compulsion [155] what you are doing of your own free will

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, AN EPIGRAM ON THE AMOURS.
s: The unit concerns the Amours, described as a work that once consisted of five books and now consists of three. The author has preferred this work to the former version by removing two books. Although reading it may no longer give the reader pleasure, the reduced work requires less labour to read.

l: Elegies, The Amores, or Amours, AN EPIGRAM ON THE AMOURS.
s: The Amours is described as having been reduced from five books to three, with two books removed. The work has been preferred by its author in this shortened form, which requires less labour to read.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, AN EPIGRAM ON THE AMOURS.
s: Naso is associated with the five books that formerly constituted the work; only three remain in the present version.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY I.
s: The poet begins by intending to write about arms and warfare in serious hexameters. Cupid interrupts by removing a metrical foot from every second line and then shoots the poet with an arrow. The poet consequently falls in love and abandons warfare for poetry in six-foot lines that close in five. He dedicates his new elegiac work to Love and wears myrtle around his temples.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY I.
s: The poet prepares to write about arms and warfare but complains when Cupid alters his verse and gives him a subject of love. After Cupid shoots him, he burns with love and begins composing in six feet followed by five.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY I.
s: Cupid smiles, removes one foot from the poet’s second verse, and changes the poet’s intended meter. He then draws his bow, shoots the poet with an unerring arrow, and compels him to write about love.

l: love poetry, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY I.
s: Love poetry becomes the poet’s subject after Cupid’s intervention. It is written in a form in which the work begins in six feet and closes in five.

l: warfare, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY I.
s: Warfare is the poet’s original subject, intended for serious verse. The poet bids farewell to warfare after Cupid turns him toward love.

l: heroic measure, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY I.
s: Epic verse is associated with the poet’s initial plan to write about arms and impetuous warfare in serious numbers. Cupid disrupts that plan by diminishing the poet’s metrical line.

l: elegiac verse, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY I.
s: Elegiac verse emerges when Cupid changes the poet’s meter and subject. It is characterized here by six feet in one line and five in the closing line.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Elegy II presents the narrator as newly conquered by Cupid and choosing to submit rather than resist Love. He imagines Cupid celebrating a triumph in which the narrator and the forces opposed to Love are led as captives, while Cupid is honored with a chariot, attendants, and acclaim. Elegy III has the narrator ask his beloved mistress either to love him or to give him a reason to continue loving her. He claims constancy, modesty, poetic talent, and a desire to have their names joined in song.

l: Elegy II, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Elegy II describes the narrator's recognition that Cupid has wounded and conquered him. It presents his submission to Love and imagines Cupid's splendid triumph over captives and enemies of Love.

l: Elegy III, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Elegy III contains the narrator's plea that the beloved mistress accept his love. He argues that his constancy, good character, poetic gifts, and love make him deserving of her favor.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The narrator suffers sleeplessness and bodily pain before realizing that Love has attacked him. He yields to Cupid, calls himself Cupid's newly made captive, and asks his beloved mistress to return his affection; he also offers lifelong fidelity and lasting poetic praise.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Cupid secretly wounds the narrator with his arrows and torments him with Love. Cupid is portrayed as a conqueror who leads captives in triumph, overcoming men and Gods with the aid of caresses, error, and madness.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The beloved mistress has recently captivated the narrator. He asks her either to love him or to give him a reason to continue loving her, and he promises to remain devoted to her and unite her name with his in song.

l: Cupid's triumph, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Cupid's triumph is imagined as a splendid procession with myrtle, his mother's doves, a chariot, captive youths and fair women, and the narrator bearing his recent wound and chains. Soundness of understanding, shame, and other enemies of Love are led bound, while the crowd and Cupid's attendants acclaim him.

l: love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The narrator's love is sudden, painful, and constant. He says that resisting it would intensify the flame, so he accepts its servitude and declares that a thousand other damsels have no charm for him compared with the beloved mistress.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The speaker, who is the lover, instructs his mistress how to behave at a banquet attended by her husband. He tells her to communicate with him through gestures, touch his foot, share wine discreetly, and avoid showing affection to her husband. He fears the husband's physical advances and sexual intimacy with the mistress, especially after the banquet, and asks her to assure him the next day that she did not enjoy them.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The speaker is jealous and distressed that the mistress's husband will attend the same banquet. He gives the mistress detailed instructions for secretly communicating with him, avoiding her husband, and arranging an opportunity after the husband is asleep. He expects the mistress to tell him the next day that she did not dally with her husband.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The mistress is instructed to arrive early, recline beside her husband modestly, touch the speaker's foot, exchange secret signs, and share wine with him discreetly. She is told to reject food tasted by her husband, prevent his embraces and kisses, and walk near the speaker when the guests leave. At home, she is expected to submit unwillingly to her husband and report afterward that she did not enjoy the encounter.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The husband attends the banquet and reclines beside the mistress. The speaker fears that he will touch, embrace, kiss, and pursue sexual intimacy with her, and advises her to make him drink until he falls asleep. The husband will later lock the mistress in and may attempt to take kisses and further intimacy from her.

l: banquet, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The banquet is attended by the speaker, the mistress, and her husband. It provides the setting for the speaker and mistress to exchange secret signs, share wine, and avoid detection. When the guests leave, the speaker instructs the mistress to walk in the middle of the crowd so that they can touch.

l: wine, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The wine is mixed and served by the husband, while the mistress is instructed to ask a servant quietly for the wine she wants. The speaker plans to drink from the cup after the mistress has sipped from it. The mistress is also told to urge her husband to drink continually and to add wine to his drink by stealth until he falls asleep.

l: secret communication, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The speaker and mistress are to communicate without speaking through glances, nods, facial expressions, eyebrow movements, finger signs traced in wine, and touches. The mistress is told to touch the speaker's foot secretly and to interpret and return his signals. These signs are intended to conceal their relationship from the husband and the other guests.

l: dalliance, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The speaker recalls that he and the mistress have often anticipated their hurried dalliance by joining hands beneath clothing. He fears that the mistress might repeat such conduct with her husband, although he says he believes she will not. He asks her to remove the covering from her bosom so that she will not even appear to be engaging in such behavior with him.

l: kissing, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The mistress is told not to kiss her husband, because the speaker says that seeing her do so would reveal him as her lover and provoke him to attack the husband. After the mistress returns home, the speaker expects the husband to take kisses from her. He asks her to receive them reluctantly, without audible caresses, and to assure him afterward that she did not enjoy them.

l: sexual intimacy, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The speaker fears that the husband will obtain sexual intimacy with the mistress after locking her in for the night. He tells her to submit only as though compelled, without pleasure or audible caresses, and wishes that the husband will find no satisfaction. He is tormented by the possibility because he has previously engaged in similar intimate conduct with the mistress.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The narrator describes a midday encounter with Corinna during summer. Corinna enters his chamber in a loose tunic, and he undresses her despite her apparent attempt to remain covered. He praises her unblemished body, embraces her, and says that they later recline, wearied, wishing for such a midday again.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: Corinna comes to the narrator's chamber wearing a loose tunic, with her flowing hair covering her white neck. She struggles to remain covered but is overcome, and the narrator describes her body as entirely without blemish before embracing her.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The narrator rests on a couch at midday and draws aside Corinna's tunic when she enters. He observes and praises her body, presses her to himself, and later reclines with her in weariness.

l: tryst (narrator and Corinna), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The tryst takes place in the narrator's chamber at summer midday, under dim light from a partly open window. The narrator and Corinna undress, embrace, and afterward recline together, and the narrator wishes for such encounters to happen often.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The lover begs the porter to open the door of his mistress's house and repeatedly asks him to strike away the bar. He recalls that Love made him brave, and he tries entreaties, promises, threats, wine, and finally considers using his sword and torch. The porter never opens the door, and the lover remains outside through the night until dawn approaches. He bids farewell to the porter, the door-posts, and the doors, lamenting the time he has wasted.

l: porter, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The porter is fastened with a cruel fetter and refuses to open the door despite the lover's repeated appeals. The lover reminds him that he once defended him before his mistress when the porter was trembling before a whip, but the porter remains unmoved and is called hard-hearted, deaf, sluggish, and worthless.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The mistress is the woman whose house the lover seeks to enter. The lover recalls having spoken to her in the porter's behalf, and he supposes that she may now be asleep with the porter.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: Cupid, together with his graceful mother, once laughed when the lover feared the night and ghosts, telling him that he too would become bold. The lover says that Cupid is with him now and that he could never send Love away without being separated from his own limbs.

l: mistress's house, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The mistress's house is the place the lover attempts to enter during the night. He threatens to scale its arrogant structure with his sword and torch if the porter will not open it.

l: door (mistress's door), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The door remains shut despite the lover's tears, entreaties, and threats. He mistakes a creaking hinge and a shaking door for a sign that it is opening, but attributes the movement to the boisterous wind, and he finally bids farewell to the doors as hard-hearted blocks of wood.

l: door-post, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The lover repeatedly asks the porter to strike the bar away from the door-post. He says that the door-posts are supported by hard oak and later bids farewell to them, calling them cruel and stubborn.

l: night, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The night passes while the lover waits outside the door, and the city becomes silent as the hours grow damp with dew. At its end, Lucifer begins moving his frost-covered wheels and a bird awakens mortals to their work.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: The speaker repents after beating his mistress and wishes to be punished for injuring her. He recalls her fear, tears, disordered hair, and pale appearance, and asks her to retaliate against him. In the next elegy, he overhears Dipsas advising a damsel to pursue wealthy lovers through deception, rivalry, pretended affection, and repeated demands for gifts and payments. The speaker is enraged by Dipsas's instructions and curses her.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: The speaker admits that frenzy raised his arms against his mistress and that he injured her by tearing her hair and marking her cheeks with his nails. He regrets his violence, calls his hands impious, wishes to be chained, and invites his mistress to punish him in return.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: The mistress weeps after being hurt by the speaker, silently condemns him through her features and tears, and repels his hands when he tries to throw himself at her feet. Her hair is disordered, her cheeks are hurt, and she becomes pale and faint with fear.

l: the beating of the mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: The beating is presented as an act of frenzy and criminal violence for which the speaker believes he deserves chains and punishment. The speaker compares his offense unfavorably with violence committed against enemies or divine beings because he injured the woman he claimed to love.

l: Dipsas, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: Dipsas is described as an old hag skilled in magic, incantations, and other occult practices. She advises the damsel to attract wealthy lovers, deceive them, provoke jealousy, pretend affection, demand gifts, and use servants and relatives to extract money. The speaker overhears her and curses her.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: The damsel is praised as beautiful but told that she lacks suitable wealth and clothing. Dipsas instructs her to entertain multiple lovers, manipulate their emotions, refuse or grant favors strategically, and secure presents and payments from them.

l: Venus, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: Dipsas says that Venus now favors the damsel because Mars has gone, and that Venus holds sway in the City of Æneas. She also claims that Venus gives a deaf hearing to lovers who have been deceived.

l: the courtesan's trade, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: The courtesan's trade is portrayed through Dipsas's instructions on attracting and managing wealthy lovers. It depends on beauty, calculated refusals, pretended affection, jealousy, deception, perjury, and the continual pursuit of material gain.

l: the lovers, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: The lovers are treated as sources of profit who should be attracted, deceived, kept uncertain, and made jealous. Dipsas advises admitting those who bring gifts, refusing those who merely plead, pretending anger, and maintaining rivalry so that their love does not fade.

l: the presents and payments extracted from lovers, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VII.
s: Dipsas urges the damsel to demand presents, accept men redeemed at a price, solicit loans that will never be returned, and enlist servants, relatives, and a nurse in gathering money. She recommends using birthdays, gifts from other men, and talk of the Sacred Street to encourage further payments.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: The speaker tells Atticus that every lover is a soldier and that Love has its own camp, since lovers endure sleepless nights, long marches, harsh weather, sieges, dangers, and watchfulness like soldiers. He argues that Love requires discernment rather than mere laziness, citing Achilles, Hector, Agamemnon, and Mars as figures affected by desire. The speaker says that Love roused him from idleness and commanded him to serve in its camp, making him active by night.

l: Atticus, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Atticus is addressed as the recipient of the speaker’s argument that every lover is a soldier and that Love is a form of warfare.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Cupid is said to have a camp of his own, making every lover a soldier in his service.

l: Love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Love is presented as a species of warfare that demands endurance, vigilance, and discernment rather than mere slothfulness. Love commands the speaker to serve in its camp and makes him active by night.

l: warfare, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Warfare is used as the central comparison for love: lovers and soldiers both endure sleeplessness, hardship, marches, watchfulness, sieges, and attacks.

l: anxious lover, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: The lover is compared to a soldier, enduring sleepless nights, sleeping on the ground, following a distant beloved, facing harsh weather, watching a rival, and besieging an obdurate mistress. Lovers also take advantage of sleeping husbands and evade sentinels and patrols.

l: soldier, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: The soldier keeps watch at a general’s door, undertakes long marches, faces cold, snow, rain, and storms, spies on the enemy, lays siege to cities, and attacks sleeping foes. The text says that an old man serving as a soldier is shocking.

l: Mars, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Mars is described as wayward and, when caught, as having experienced the chains made at the forge. His story is said to be widely known throughout the heavens.

l: Venus, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Venus is described as uncertain, like Mars, because in both love and war the defeated may rise again and those thought incapable of falling may be overthrown.

l: Achilles, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Achilles is said to have been inflamed by the captive Briseis.

l: Briseis, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Briseis is identified as the captive who inflamed Achilles.

l: Trojans, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: The Trojans are urged to destroy the Argive resources while they have the opportunity.

l: Hector, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Hector used to go to battle immediately after embracing Andromache.

l: Andromache, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Andromache placed Hector’s helmet on his head before he went to battle.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The speaker tells his mistress that requiring presents has destroyed his former love for her. He argues that love should be naked, childlike, and free from sordid payment, unlike prostitution or bribery. He says that sexual pleasure is shared equally by woman and man and should not be sold by one to the other. The speaker offers duty, zeal, fidelity, and poetry instead of money, promising lasting fame to the woman he chooses.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The mistress once pleased the speaker because she was disinterested, but her demand for presents has blemished her disposition in his estimation. He asks her to stop demanding payment and says that he will then give her what he refuses while she asks for it.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The speaker says that he formerly loved his mistress's mind as well as her person, but that her requests for presents have cured his passion. He offers duty, zeal, fidelity, and poetic praise as what he can give her.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: Love is described as both a child and naked, with years but without sordidness or concealment. The speaker asks why the son of Venus should be prostituted at a price, since Love is unsuited to serve for pay.

l: gifts and presents, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The mistress requires gifts and presents as a return for her love, and this requirement causes the speaker to reject her appearance and disposition. The speaker says that a present may appropriately be requested from a wealthy man, while a needy man should offer duty, zeal, and fidelity.

l: payment for sexual favors, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The text condemns making sexual favors a matter of payment. It compares this practice with prostitution, bribery, and purchased testimony, and says that once a man has paid, he no longer remains a debtor for the woman's acquiescence.

l: disinterested love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The speaker says that he loved his mistress when she was disinterested. He presents love without demands for presents as genuine, while treating love that is bargained for as corrupted by payment.

l: woman, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The text says that woman alone among the animals takes pleasure in spoils taken from man, lets out her nights, and sells sexual pleasure for a price. It also says that a woman may appropriately receive a gift from a wealthy man, but should not bargain for payment for her favors.

l: Delights of Love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: Sexual pleasure is described as a joy that delights both woman and man and that both desire. The speaker questions why one should sell and the other buy a pleasure for which both combine with kindred impulse.

l: poetry, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The speaker says that his endowments lie in his lines and that he can sing the praises of fair women who deserve them. Through his poetic skill, the woman he chooses becomes celebrated.

l: fame, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The fame conferred by poetry is said to be everlasting, unlike vestments, gems, and gold, which will rend or spoil. The speaker offers lasting fame rather than payment for sexual favors.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XI.
s: The speaker asks Nape to deliver his inscribed tablets to Corinna and urges her to overcome any delay. He instructs Nape to observe Corinna's reaction, have her read the tablets immediately, and request a long reply, though he would be satisfied if she wrote only "Come." Corinna instead sends back a letter refusing to be seen that day. The speaker then curses the tablets, blaming their unlucky material and color for carrying her refusal.

l: Nape, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XI.
s: Nape is praised for arranging hair neatly, managing secret nighttime arrangements, giving signals, and faithfully helping the speaker in his difficulties. The speaker asks her to deliver his tablets to Corinna and obtain a reply.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XI.
s: Corinna is Nape's mistress and the recipient of the speaker's tablets. She refuses the speaker's request, sending word that she cannot be seen that day.

l: tablets, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XI.
s: The tablets carry the speaker's persuasive writing to Corinna. They return with a letter of refusal, after which the speaker curses them, calls them fatal and useless, and imagines that their wood came from a tree associated with execution and birds of ill omen.

l: letter, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XI.
s: The letter is written by Corinna on the tablets and announces that she cannot be seen that day. The speaker wants Corinna to write a long answer, although he says that the single word "Come" would be enough.

l: Nape delivering the tablets, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XI.
s: Nape is instructed to take the well-filled tablets to Corinna that morning and deliver them without delay. She is also told to make Corinna read them at once, watch her expression, and ask her to write a reply.

l: Corinna's refusal, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XI.
s: Corinna's refusal is conveyed in her letter, which says that she cannot be seen that day. The refusal causes the speaker to lament his misfortune and curse the tablets that carried the message.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: The speaker begs Aurora not to hasten the arrival of morning because he is enjoying sleep and the company of his mistress. He criticizes Aurora for waking sailors, travelers, soldiers, farmers, children, lawyers, advocates, and workers. He recalls her passion for Cephalus and contrasts her conduct with the extra nights the Moon and Jupiter once granted to their lovers. Aurora blushes at his reproaches, but the day still rises no later than usual.

l: Aurora, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Aurora comes from her aged husband Tithonus in a frosty chariot and brings on the day. The speaker urges her to restrain her dewy reins and delay, reproaching her for disturbing lovers and waking people to their labors. He accuses her of avoiding Tithonus because of his age and recalls her former passion for Cephalus; she blushes at his words, but does not delay the day.

l: morning, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Morning arrives when Aurora rises and interrupts the speaker's sleep and pleasure with his mistress. Its approach wakes sailors, travelers, soldiers, farmers, children, lawyers, advocates, and wool-workers to their duties.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: The mistress lies beside the speaker in the soft arms of sleep and is deliciously united with him. Her early rising is the chief reason he begs Aurora not to hasten.

l: night, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Night gives the speaker sleep and time with his mistress, so he wishes it would not make way for Aurora. He imagines the horses of the night being told to run slowly, and recalls that Jupiter joined two nights together to fulfill his desires.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The mistress has nearly lost her hair after repeatedly treating it with noxious compositions, despite the speaker's earlier warnings. He recalls that her natural hair was abundant, fine, manageable, and beautiful, but that she subjected it to bodkins, combs, iron, and fire. He explains that the damage was self-inflicted rather than caused by magic, illness, or envy, and predicts that captured German hair will be used to adorn her. The mistress is ashamed of relying on bought hair, but the speaker comforts her that her natural hair may eventually grow back.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The mistress repeatedly treated her hair despite the speaker's warnings to leave it alone. After nearly losing it, she becomes distressed and ashamed, looks at her former locks placed in her bosom, and is told that her natural hair may eventually return.

l: hair, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The mistress's former hair was abundant, fine, soft, naturally mixed in colour, easy to manage, and long enough to reach down her sides. It endured combing, bodkins, iron, and fire until the tortured hair was lost; the speaker compares it to hair desired by Apollo, Bacchus, and Dione.

l: noxious hair-dyeing compositions, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The noxious compositions were repeatedly applied to the mistress's head and helped cause the loss of her hair. The speaker says that no rival's herbs, hag's water, disease, or envious tongue was responsible.

l: hair dyeing and treatment, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The mistress's hair treatment included dyeing, dressing, combing, use of a bodkin, and curling with iron and fire. The speaker condemns these practices as harmful and urges her to stop using violence against her hair.

l: hair loss, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The mistress has nearly become bald because her own treatment damaged and removed her hair. She mourns the loss, but the speaker says it may still be repaired and that she may soon become beautiful with natural hair.

l: captured German hair, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: Captured German hair will be sent to the mistress and used to adorn her in place of her lost natural hair. She will receive praise for this bought hair while feeling that the praise belongs to an unknown Sygambrian girl rather than to herself.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: The speaker answers Envy by defending poetry as a pursuit that seeks everlasting fame rather than perishable military or legal honors. He argues that poets including the Mæonian bard, the Ascræan, Sophocles, Menander, Ennius, Lucretius, and others will be remembered for as long as the world endures. Rome will remain associated with Tityrus, the harvests, and the arms of Æneas while it rules the conquered earth. The speaker concludes that poetry will survive monarchs, triumphs, wealth, and even death.

l: Envy, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: Envy blames the speaker for years of slothfulness and calls poetry the employment of an idle mind. Envy feeds upon the living but rests after death, when each person’s merit protects his reward.

l: poetry, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: Poetry seeks everlasting fame and is exempt from death. It is presented as capable of outlasting monarchs, their triumphs, wealth, flint-stones, and the enduring plough.

l: fame, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: Fame is sought so that the speaker may be celebrated throughout the whole world and remembered for all time. The fame of numerous poets is said to endure as long as natural and human things continue to exist.

l: Mæonian bard, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: The Mæonian bard will live as long as Tenedos and Ida stand and as long as the Simois rolls its waves to the sea.

l: Rome, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: Rome is described as the ruler of the conquered earth. As long as Rome holds that rule, Tityrus, the harvests, and the arms of Æneas will be read of.

l: Death, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: Death does not destroy poetry, which remains alive after the speaker’s closing fire has consumed him. After death, Envy is at rest and each person’s merit protects his reward.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Naso says that Love and Cupid have made him write about love instead of the wars of heaven and the Giants. He recounts abandoning Jupiter and his thunderbolts when his mistress shut her door against him, because gentle Elegies and verses won access where force could not. He declares that verses have magical power and that singing of a beautiful fair being can win her as the Poet’s reward. He invites young lovers and charming fair women to read his lines, while warning prudish matrons away.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Naso identifies himself as born among the watery Peligni and as the Poet of his own failings. He says he began to sing of the battles of heaven and the Giants, but turned to love poetry after his mistress shut her door against him; his gentle words and Elegies then prevailed.

l: Book the Second Elegy I, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Book the Second Elegy I presents Naso’s explanation for writing about Love instead of the wars of heaven and the Giants. It addresses young lovers and charming fair women while excluding prudish matrons.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Cupid demands this work from Naso and dictates the lines about love to him. Cupid is described as wounding youths with his bow, including Naso.

l: Love, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Love demands that Naso compose this work rather than continue with his earlier subject of heavenly battles.

l: warfare, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: The wars, specifically the battles of the heavens, were the subject Naso had begun to sing about before Love redirected him to love poetry.

l: Jove, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Jove would have hurled his lightnings in defense of the realms of heaven while Naso sang of the Giants. Naso abandoned Jove and his weapons when his mistress shut her door, and he asks Jove to pardon him.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Naso’s mistress shut her door against him while he was preparing to sing of the battles of heaven. Her rejection caused him to abandon Jove and resume writing affectionate Elegies, whose gentle words eventually prevailed.

l: door (mistress's door), The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: The door shut against Naso was more potent to him than Jove’s thunderbolt. Naso says that his gentle words overcame the obdurate door and its oak bar.

l: Elegies, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Naso resumes his language of endearment and trifling Elegies after abandoning his earlier subject. These Elegies serve as his own weapons and help him prevail over the obdurate door.

l: verses, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Naso attributes extraordinary power to verses: they can bring down the blood-stained Moon’s horns, recall the Sun’s snow-white steeds, make serpents burst, reverse flowing water, and open barred doors. Verses also win the beautiful fair being as a reward for the Poet.

l: beautiful fair being, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: The beautiful fair being is often sung by the Poet, and she presents herself to him as the reward for his verse.

l: charming fair, The Amores, or Amours, BOOK THE SECOND ELEGY I.
s: Naso calls on the charming fair to turn their eyes to his lines, which Cupid dictates to him.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Ovid addresses Bagous, the eunuch assigned to watch his mistress, after the mistress refuses Ovid's request to visit her because of Bagous's strict surveillance. He urges Bagous to relax his watch and secretly aid the mistress's meetings by overlooking letters, visitors, absences, and visits to temples or theatres. Ovid argues that informers and accusers are punished or distrusted, while a husband is likely either indifferent or made miserable by accusations. He presents the proposed affair as harmless because it involves neither poison nor violence, only a wish to love and meet safely.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Ovid has seen a young lady walking in the portico of the temple of Apollo and has sent her a request to visit her. He addresses Bagous, urging him to relax his surveillance and help the lovers meet safely. He argues that accusations harm either an indifferent husband or a husband who dotes on his wife.

l: Bagous, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Bagous is the eunuch charged with watching his mistress. Ovid urges him to become a confidant by overlooking letters, male visitors, unexplained absences, and visits to temples or theatres. If Bagous helps conceal the affair and keeps silent, Ovid says he may gain honour, increase his savings, and eventually become free.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The mistress is the young lady whom Ovid sees walking in the portico of the temple of Apollo. She refuses Ovid's request because Bagous watches her too strictly. Ovid suggests that she may secretly receive visitors, read letters, visit supposedly sick female friends, attend sacrifices, or go to the temple of Isis and the theatres.

l: husband (Corinna's husband), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The mistress's husband is described as irrationally concerned with guarding what would not be lost even without surveillance. Ovid says that the husband may believe the mistress chaste because she pleases everyone, and that her tears and denials may make him distrust his own eyes and punish an informer.

l: surveillance of the mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The surveillance of the mistress is so strict that she tells Ovid she cannot receive him. Ovid argues that such watchfulness is unnecessary and encourages Bagous to appear vigilant while secretly overlooking the mistress's conduct.

l: secret affair, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The secret affair concerns Ovid's wish to meet and love the mistress while concealing the relationship from her husband. Ovid advises Bagous and the mistress to use plausible explanations, feigned accusations, tears, and silence to hide what is really happening.

l: love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Ovid asks that Bagous enable him and the mistress to love and meet safely. He insists that their request is harmless because they are not mixing poisons or carrying drawn swords.

l: accusations, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: Ovid says accusations please no husband: an indifferent husband will not care, while a devoted husband will be made miserable. Informers may be chained or imprisoned, and the example of Tantalus shows the danger of a blabbing tongue; Ovid also mentions a keeper of Io who died before his time and another informer who suffered fetters while the woman lost her character.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The poet addresses Bagous, who guards his mistress and has resisted the poet’s request, by sympathizing with his inability to experience mutual love. He urges Bagous to abandon manly pursuits, serve his mistress, and seek her favor while the opportunity remains. The poet then confesses that he is attracted to every kind of fair woman, finding charm in differences of character, appearance, age, talent, and manner. He concludes that his passion desires whatever qualities people admire in women throughout the City.

l: Bagous, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: Bagous watches his mistress but, being neither man nor woman, cannot experience the mutual transports of love. The poet urges him to abandon manly aspirations, serve his mistress, and overwhelm her with favors, warning that she may deceive him despite his watchfulness.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: Bagous's mistress is described as beautiful and of an age suited for dalliance, so her charms should not fade through neglect. The poet says that she may deceive Bagous, but that her gratitude might benefit him if he serves her.

l: charming fair, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: Fair women attract the poet in every variety: modest or forward, prudish or learned, simple or accomplished, tall or short, adorned or unadorned, blonde or brunette, youthful or mature. He finds their different manners, voices, movements, talents, and appearances sufficient to inspire his passion.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The poet confesses that he cannot control his attraction to women and compares himself to a ship carried along by a rapid tide. He admits that he is pleased by women who praise or abuse him and that he is excited on every occasion.

l: love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: Love is presented as a force that the poet cannot rule or resist. It can be awakened by any of a hundred forms of beauty, character, talent, age, or behavior.

l: beauty, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: Beauty appears in many forms, including modesty, liveliness, learning, simplicity, graceful movement, singing, skilled playing, height, shortness, adornment, hair color, complexion, youth, and maturity. The poet finds no single style of beauty necessary for passion.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The speaker confronts his mistress after witnessing her secretly communicating and exchanging passionate kisses with a rival. He recalls their gestures, coded words, and behavior at the table, which reveal her guilt and infidelity. Though angered and tempted to hurt her, he is disarmed by her beauty and instead begs for kisses like those she gave the rival. Her kisses are so skilled and delightful that he suspects she learned them through closer acquaintance with someone else.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The speaker witnesses his mistress communicating secretly with another person and later kissing him. He becomes angry and jealous, but her beauty weakens his resolve, so he begs her for kisses and remains tormented by the possibility that she gave the rival equally good ones.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The mistress is accused of acting falsely toward the speaker. She communicates with the rival through gestures, coded words, and glances, kisses him passionately, blushes when confronted, and then gives the speaker unusually skillful kisses.

l: rival (mistress's other lover), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The rival is the person with whom the mistress exchanges secret signs and passionate kisses. The speaker fears that the rival received kisses equal to those the mistress gives him.

l: guilt and infidelity, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The mistress’s guilt is revealed through the speaker’s direct observation rather than erased tablets or secret presents. Her gestures, coded conversation, and kisses with the rival serve as evidence of her infidelity.

l: jealousy and grief, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The speaker’s jealousy and grief make him wish to die whenever he remembers the mistress’s guilt. They provoke anger and thoughts of attacking her, but they continue afterward because he fears that the rival received kisses of equal quality.

l: kisses, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY V.
s: The mistress gives the rival passionate kisses and later gives the speaker kisses that are exceptionally powerful, delightful, and more skillful than those he taught her. Their quality makes the speaker suspect that she learned them through a closer acquaintance with someone else.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The speaker laments the death of the parrot he gave to Corinna and calls on the birds to mourn it. He praises the parrot's plumage, peaceful nature, frugal habits, and skill at imitating human speech, noting that it died after crying, "Corinna, farewell!" The parrot is imagined among innocent birds at the foot of the Elysian hill, where a small sepulchre bears an inscription honoring its devotion to its mistress and its eloquence. The speaker then protests Corinna's repeated accusations and denies that he had an affair with her handmaid Cypassis.

l: parrot, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The parrot, sent from the Indians of the East, was given to Corinna and became the speaker's subject of mourning after its death. It had beautiful plumage, a purple beak, a talent for imitating human speech, peaceful habits, and a diet of nuts, poppies, and pure water. As it died, it cried, "Corinna, farewell!" and was imagined among innocent birds at the foot of the Elysian hill, where a small sepulchre commemorated its devotion and eloquence.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: Corinna was the speaker's mistress, and the parrot had pleased her since it was given to her. She anxiously prayed for the parrot during its illness, and the dying bird addressed her in its final words. She also repeatedly accused the speaker of finding other women attractive and of having an affair with Cypassis.

l: birds, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The birds are summoned to attend the parrot's obsequies, mourn with their wings and claws, and replace their sorrowing hair with torn feathers. Innocent birds are said to dwell near the Elysian hill, while obscene birds are expelled; swans, the Phoenix, Juno's bird, and doves are mentioned there.

l: turtle-dove, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The turtle-dove is urged to mourn the parrot above the other birds. The two had maintained a firm, lasting attachment throughout life, and the turtle-dove is compared to the companion of Orestes.

l: Elysian hill, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: At the foot of the Elysian hill there is a grove of dark holm oaks and earth covered with ever-living grass. It is described as the dwelling place of innocent birds, where the dead parrot is imagined to attract other guileless birds with its words.

l: sepulchre, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: A small sepulchre covers the parrot's bones. Its inscription says that the parrot had been its mistress's favorite and possessed a tongue more skilled at talking than those of other birds.

l: death of the parrot, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The death of the parrot is presented as a major cause of sorrow, and the birds are called to mourn it. The parrot died on a day that would have no tomorrow, with its Destiny's distaff uncovered, but it retained enough voice to say, "Corinna, farewell!"

l: accusation, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: The speaker complains that Corinna continually brings new accusations against him. He says she interprets his looks, praise, blame, and changes in health as evidence of love for another woman, and he rejects the accusation that he had a sexual relationship with Cypassis.

l: Cypassis, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VI.
s: Cypassis is Corinna's handmaid, skilled at arranging hair and valuable for the work of her hands. Corinna accuses her of supplanting her with the speaker, but the speaker denies desiring or having sexual intercourse with her.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VIII.
s: Corinna discovers the speaker’s affair with Cypassis, her handmaid, and reacts angrily. The speaker defends the affair by denying that he revealed it and by citing famous men who loved enslaved or captive women. He then asks Cypassis for her company and threatens to expose their earlier meetings if she refuses.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VIII.
s: Corinna learns of the speaker’s intrigue with Cypassis and fixes angry eyes upon Cypassis. The speaker tries to persuade Corinna that he gave no guilty sign of their secret amours.

l: Cypassis, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VIII.
s: Cypassis is Corinna’s handmaid and is highly skilled at arranging hair in many fashions. The speaker describes her as experienced in their intrigue, asks her to reward him with her company, and threatens to reveal their past meetings if she refuses.

l: the affair between the speaker and Cypassis, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY VIII.
s: The affair consists of stolen and secret caresses between the speaker and Cypassis. Corinna discovers it, and the speaker threatens to disclose where, how often, and in how many ways he and Cypassis have met.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: The speaker addresses Cupid, complaining that Cupid wounds and torments a loyal soldier while sparing those who resist him. The speaker compares his love-sickness to the exhaustion of soldiers, horses, ships, and weapons after service, yet admits that he would refuse release from love because the fair are such a sweet evil. He asks Cupid to resume attacking him and describes the uncertainty of his mistress’s affection as a source of both hope and misery. He finally asks Cupid, with his mother, to rule his heart and extend his realm over the damsels.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Cupid has taken up residence in the speaker’s heart, torments him, wounds him with his bow and torch, and leaves his bones bare through Love. Although Cupid’s followers are well acquainted with his weapons, his hand is said to slacken against resisting foes; the speaker asks him to direct his strength at the speaker instead. Cupid is described as fickle, giving and refusing joys at will, and as influencing the uncertain warfare of Mars.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: The speaker presents himself as Cupid’s loyal soldier, wounded in Cupid’s own camp despite never deserting his standards. He says he is exhausted from serving love and ought to be discharged, but he would refuse a life without love because the fair are a sweet evil. He asks Cupid to pierce him while he is unarmed and exposed, and he hopes for alternating caresses, reproaches, favor, and rejection from his mistress.

l: Love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Love has left the speaker’s bones quite bare and causes him to be bewildered when passion fades from his mind. The speaker describes Love as an uncertain force that repeatedly carries him away and makes him resume his familiar weapons.

l: damsels, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IX.
s: Some damsels are free from Love and could be conquered by Cupid in a glorious triumph. The speaker asks that the damsels, whom he considers far too flighty, be added to Cupid’s realms so that two peoples may revere him.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The speaker tells Græcinus that he is in love with two mistresses at the same time, and that his feelings fluctuate between them. He celebrates his devotion to Love and wishes to die in Love's service. He tries to dissuade Corinna from sailing to Baiæ by describing the dangers of the ocean, though he promises to welcome her ship if she returns safely. He then celebrates his success in overcoming the obstacles guarding Corinna and compares it to a triumph won through his own efforts.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The speaker admits to Græcinus that he is simultaneously in love with two mistresses and is tormented by choosing between them. He wishes to remain devoted to Love, to die in Love's service, and to be remembered as having met a fitting death. He urges Corinna not to sail, promises to welcome her return, and claims sole credit for overcoming the obstacles that guarded her.

l: two mistresses, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The two mistresses are both charming, attentive to their dress, and apparently equal in skill and beauty. The speaker's passion shifts between them, leaving him distracted, but he says that either one might be enough to cause him to die with love.

l: Love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: Love continually disturbs the speaker's sleep and causes him to endure passionate struggles. The speaker prefers suffering from Love to living a serious or solitary life and wishes to die while serving Love.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: Corinna prepares to leave her familiar couch and household gods to travel by sea to Baiæ. The speaker fears for her safety, urges her to remain on land, and later hopes that she will return safely so that he can embrace and kiss her.

l: ocean, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The ocean is portrayed as deceitful, dangerous, and unchanging in appearance. It contains storms, hazardous rocks and straits, and waves that make sailors fear death; its middle lacks the shells and colored pebbles found on the shore.

l: ship (speaker's safely returned vessel), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: Corinna's ship travels onto the boundless ocean after its cable is loosened, exposing those aboard to storms and peril. The speaker hopes to be the first to recognize it when it returns and prays for favorable winds to fill its sails.

l: Triumph, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: The speaker calls for triumphant laurels and invites Triumph to come to him because he has obtained Corinna without bloodshed. His victory is presented as a personal achievement rather than one shared with soldiers.

l: Cupid, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: Cupid orders the speaker, along with many others, to carry the standard in his service. The speaker presents himself as participating in Cupid's warfare without bloodshed.

l: the speaker's warfare, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY X.
s: Love's warfare concerns the pursuit and possession of women rather than the conquest of cities. The speaker compares his success in overcoming Corinna's husband, keeper, and strong door with famous conflicts caused by women, while emphasizing that his own victory involved no bloodshed.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Corinna lies exhausted and in danger of her life while attempting to deliver the burden of her pregnant womb. Naso believes that he may be the father of the child and fears for Corinna despite being angry that she undertook the risk without his knowledge. He prays to Isis and Lucina, or Ilithyia, to save Corinna and promises offerings and an inscription in her honor. He urges Corinna not to undergo such a struggle again.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Corinna is exhausted and lies prostrate in danger of her life while trying to disengage the burden of her pregnant womb. Naso says that she conceived by him, or so he thinks, and prays that she will survive.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Naso is angry that Corinna undertook the risk without his knowledge, but his anger gives way to apprehension. He prays to Isis and Lucina for Corinna's life and promises frankincense, vowed gifts, and an inscription in their honor.

l: Isis, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Isis is invoked as a goddess associated with Parætonium, Canopus, Memphis, Pharos, and the Nile. Naso asks her to turn her attention toward Corinna and have mercy on both Corinna and him.

l: Lucina, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Lucina is addressed as one who has compassion on females in labor. Naso asks her to come favorably and listen to his prayers for Corinna.

l: pregnancy and childbirth, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Corinna's pregnant womb carries a burden that she is trying to disengage, leaving her exhausted and in peril. Naso treats the labor as a struggle and asks that Corinna not undergo such a combat again.

l: Corinna's unborn child, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: The child is implied to have been conceived by Naso and to be the burden of Corinna's pregnant womb. Naso's appeal to Isis asks for mercy on two people by giving life to Corinna, who gives life to him.

l: danger to Corinna's life, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Corinna's attempt to deliver the pregnancy places her in danger of death. This danger causes Naso's apprehension and leads him to seek divine intervention.

l: prayer to Isis and Lucina, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIII.
s: Naso's prayer asks Isis and Lucina to save Corinna during her labor. He promises to offer frankincense and vowed gifts at their altars and to add an inscription stating that Naso offers them for Corinna's preservation.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The speaker reproaches his mistress for attempting to destroy the embryo in her womb. He argues that such an act is unnatural and recalls examples of famous mothers whose children became important figures, including Achilles, Romulus, and Aeneas. He warns that attempts to end a pregnancy can kill the woman herself and prays that his mistress will survive this transgression, while hoping she will not repeat it.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The speaker condemns the mistress's attempted abortion and compares it to unnatural acts of maternal violence. He says that he himself would never have lived if his mother had killed him before his birth, and he prays for the mistress's safety.

l: attempted abortion, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The attempted abortion is portrayed as a criminal and unnatural act that destroys a tender embryo. The speaker says it may cause the woman to die and declares that a second such transgression should receive its own punishment.

l: embryo, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The embryo is described as tender and not yet born. The speaker argues that it should be allowed to grow and compares ending its development to plucking unripe fruit or destroying the growing grapes of a loaded vine.

l: unborn child (the mistress's pregnancy), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: The unborn child is threatened by the mistress's use of instruments and poisons. The speaker presents its possible destruction as the loss of a life that might have become significant, as happened with the children associated with Achilles, Romulus, and Aeneas.

l: pregnancy and childbirth, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIV.
s: Pregnancy is presented as a condition that should be allowed to continue until the child is born, rather than being ended prematurely. The speaker says that life is a substantial reward for waiting and warns that interfering with pregnancy can bring death to the woman herself.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: The speaker addresses a ring that he is giving to his mistress and envies the ring’s opportunity to touch and be worn by her. He imagines being changed into the ring so that he could touch her bosom, seal her tablets, and remain with her. He sends the ring as a sign that his constancy is offered to his mistress.

l: ring, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: The ring is presented as a pleasing gift to the mistress and is asked to fit closely around her finger. It is imagined touching her bosom, sealing her secret tablets, and being worn while she bathes; it is also told to convey the speaker’s constancy.

l: beautiful fair being, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: The mistress is expected to receive the ring joyfully, place it on her finger, and handle it. The speaker imagines touching her bosom, sealing her tablets, and seeing her naked while she bathes.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: The speaker envies the ring because it can touch and remain close to his mistress. He wishes to be transformed into the ring and imagines escaping from her finger into her bosom, sealing her tablets, and refusing to leave her desk.

l: constancy, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XV.
s: The speaker’s constancy is described as something proffered with the ring. The ring is asked to help the mistress understand that the speaker offers her this constancy.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVI.
s: The speaker is staying at Sulmo in the Pelignian land and praises its streams, fertile fields, vines, olives, and cool air. Despite these natural delights, the speaker cannot feel happy because his mistress is far away. He says that any journey would be pleasant with his love, even across dangerous mountains and seas. He urges his mistress to visit him and asks the hills and paths to become smooth for her arrival.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVI.
s: The speaker is staying at Sulmo and admires the healthfulness and beauty of the surrounding Pelignian fields. Without his mistress, he feels as though he is not in his native place but in distant and hostile lands. He asks his mistress to join him and says he would endure any dangerous journey with his love.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVI.
s: The mistress is far away from the speaker, although she had sworn to be his companion. The speaker says that her promises are empty unless she now proves them by coming to him in her little chaise. He asks the hills and winding paths to become smooth wherever she travels.

l: Sulmo, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVI.
s: Sulmo, described as a small and salubrious place, receives the speaker. It is presented as part of the Pelignian land and is surrounded by flowing streams, fertile fields, vines, olives, and refreshing air.

l: the Pelignian fields, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVI.
s: The Pelignian land is praised for its flowing streams, verdant grass, fertile cornfields, fruitful vines, and olive trees. Its meadows, vines, and cool air cannot make the speaker happy while his mistress is absent.

l: love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVI.
s: The speaker's love is identified with the person who excites his flame and is currently far away. With his love, the speaker says that he could cross the Alps, the Libyan quicksands, and dangerous seas without fear.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVII.
s: The speaker says he is the slave of Corinna and accepts disgrace for serving her, provided she torments him less severely. He praises her beauty while criticizing her pride and asks her to accept him despite their unequal standing. He compares their relationship with other unions between mortals and divine or heroic figures. He promises that his poems will celebrate only Corinna and provide her with fame instead of wealth.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVII.
s: Corinna possesses great beauty, which makes her proud and disdainful toward the speaker. She is the only woman whom the speaker promises to celebrate in his poems.

l: tyranny, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVII.
s: The tyranny is the harsh control Corinna exercises over the speaker. He hopes that she will torment him with less violence and impose conditions while still showing affection.

l: affection, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVII.
s: The affection concerns the speaker’s devotion to Corinna. He asks her to receive him on any terms and says that their affection should not be disavowed by her.

l: poetry, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVII.
s: The poems are the speaker’s cheerful lines, which he offers Corinna in place of great wealth. They will celebrate no woman but Corinna, who alone will provide subject matter for his genius.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVIII.
s: The speaker-poet contrasts Macer's work on the wrath of Achilles and the arms of heroes with his own retreat into Venus's shade and enslavement to Love. His mistress repeatedly defeats his attempts to leave her, drawing him from tragedy and other ambitious subjects back to love poetry. He describes letters and laments concerning figures including Penelope, Phyllis, Dido, and others, many of which his friend Sabinus has brought from different parts of the world. The speaker-poet urges Macer to include Love in his poems about war, suggesting that Macer prefers these subjects as much as warfare.

l: Macer, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVIII.
s: Macer is tracing a poem about the wrath of Achilles and giving the heroes their first arms after the oaths. The speaker-poet urges him to write about Love as well as war, claiming that he does not sing of wars with greater pleasure than of love.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVIII.
s: The speaker-poet rests in the shade of Venus while Love interrupts his attempts to undertake a mighty subject. He is drawn away from tragedy and other ambitious writing, and instead composes works about tender love, letters, and abandoned lovers.

l: Love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVIII.
s: Love attacks the speaker-poet whenever he attempts a serious subject and triumphs over him as a tragic poet. Love also appears amid warfare, and the speaker-poet encourages Macer to sing of it.

l: mistress (an indulgent woman), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVIII.
s: The speaker's mistress defeats the speaker-poet's attempts to send her away by sitting in his lap, weeping, embracing him, and giving him many overpowering kisses. Her influence draws him away from tragedy and back to Love.

l: the art of tender love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVIII.
s: The speaker-poet says that he either teaches the art of tender love or writes the words and laments of lovers. He is tormented by his own precepts while teaching this art.

l: war, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XVIII.
s: War is the subject of Macer's poem about Achilles, heroes, and their arms. The speaker-poet says that even in the midst of warfare, Love can be sung, with Paris, the adultress, and Laodamia appearing alongside martial subjects.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIX.
s: The lover tells Corinna's husband that he should watch Corinna more carefully, because obstacles, refusals, and uncertainty intensify desire and preserve love. He recalls how Corinna feigned headaches and faults, then rewarded his frustration with affection, kisses, and kind words. He urges the husband to become suspicious of Corinna's movements and companions, warning that an affair freely permitted will soon cease to interest him. The lover concludes that the husband's excessive leniency is spoiling his pleasure and that he should forbid the affair if he wants the lover to remain his rival.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIX.
s: Corinna is described as clever and as having recognized the lover's attraction to difficulty. She feigned headaches and faults in order to dismiss and torment him, then restored his affection through caresses, delightful words, and kisses. The husband is encouraged to suspect her nighttime movements and possible communications.

l: love, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIX.
s: Love is said to become lasting through resistance, fear, hope, and prolonged experience. Too much indulgence and easy access make love weary, like sweet food that cloys the appetite.

l: desire, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIX.
s: Desire grows stronger when what is wanted is withheld or made difficult to obtain. The lover says that occasional repulse gives room for desire, while constant availability destroys its force.

l: jealous surveillance and restraint, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY XIX.
s: Jealous surveillance is presented as a way to create anxiety and obstacles that sustain the lover's interest. The husband is urged to investigate nighttime footsteps, barking dogs, the handmaid's tablets, and Corinna's habit of lying apart.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ---- BOOK THE THIRD. / ELEGY I.
s: The Poet walks in an ancient sacred grove and considers what work his Muse should begin. Elegy and Tragedy appear before him, with Tragedy urging him to abandon love poetry and write about heroic exploits, while Elegy defends her influence and usefulness. The Poet asks both forbearance, and Tragedy grants him a short respite to continue writing about tender Love before undertaking a greater task.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ---- BOOK THE THIRD. / ELEGY I.
s: The Poet deliberates in a sacred grove about whether to continue writing Elegies or begin a greater work of Tragedy. He asks Elegy and Tragedy to hear him without prejudice, acknowledging that Tragedy offers him lofty poetic fame while Elegy offers lasting fame for his loves. He is granted a short respite to write about tender Love before beginning the more weighty undertaking.

l: Elegy, The Amores, or Amours, ---- BOOK THE THIRD. / ELEGY I.
s: Elegy appears with perfumed hair, a humble robe, and one foot seemingly longer than the other. She defends herself against Tragedy, saying that her caressing words can open doors that Tragedy's rigid buskin cannot. She claims to have helped Corinna deceive her keeper, leave her couch at night, receive messages, and inspire the Poet's genius.

l: Tragedy, The Amores, or Amours, ---- BOOK THE THIRD. / ELEGY I.
s: Tragedy appears with a scowling brow, flowing locks, a royal sceptre, and a Lydian buskin. She reproaches the Poet for his love poetry and urges him to sing of heroes and undertake a greater task. After the Poet's entreaty, she grants him a short respite before he begins that more serious work.

l: Love, The Amores, or Amours, ---- BOOK THE THIRD. / ELEGY I.
s: Love is presented as the subject of Elegy's playful poetry, with Cupid described as Elegy's care and companion. The Poet is allowed to sketch tender Love briefly before turning to a more weighty undertaking.

l: Corinna, The Amores, or Amours, ---- BOOK THE THIRD. / ELEGY I.
s: Corinna learned through Elegy how to deceive her keeper, loosen the constancy of a fastened door, leave her couch in a loose tunic, and move through the night without stumbling. She tore apart a birthday message sent to her and threw it into the water near her home.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The speaker attends the chariot races in the Circus Maximus mainly to be near his mistress and watch her rather than the race. He flirts with her, helps adjust her clothing, and asks her to permit herself to be loved. During the race, he supports her favorite charioteer, who eventually wins after a difficult turn and a restart. The mistress signals her favor to the speaker, promising him something more in another place.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The speaker attends the Circus Maximus to sit beside his mistress and admire her, though he pretends to be concerned with the race. He tries to protect and assist her, declares his passion, supports her favorite charioteer, and receives a promising look from her.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The mistress watches the chariot race beside the speaker and is briefly pressed by the people around her. She favors one charioteer, whose victory fulfills her wishes, and she gives the speaker an encouraging sign and a promise of something more.

l: favorite charioteer, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The favorite charioteer initially drives too wide around the turning-place and is nearly overtaken. The crowd calls him back, and after the restart he wins the race, securing the palm desired by the mistress.

l: horses, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The horses race from the barriers around the Circus, with the speaker imagining himself driving and controlling them. The favorite charioteer's horses seem to understand the mistress's wishes, but they initially take a circuit that is too wide before surging forward at full speed.

l: chariot race, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The chariot race includes a procession, a first start, a call to stop and restart, and a final contest across the Circus. The mistress's favored competitor wins, while the speaker treats the victory as hers and continues seeking his own romantic victory.

l: Circus Maximus, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY II.
s: The Circus Maximus provides the setting where the speaker sits close to his mistress because of the arrangement of its seating. Its barriers, turning-place, open space, procession, crowd, and chariot race shape the events of the unit.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The speaker complains that his mistress has broken her oath to the Gods and to him, yet her beauty remains unchanged. He argues that the Gods allow beautiful women to commit perjury with impunity while men suffer punishment. The speaker questions whether the Gods exist or whether they favor charming women, recalling divine punishments inflicted on others. He finally asks the mistress to use the Gods’ favor more moderately and to show some regard for his eyes.

l: mistress, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The mistress has sworn falsely to the Gods and to the speaker, but her flowing hair, complexion, stature, feet, and expressive eyes remain as beautiful as before. She laughs unpunished at the Gods and at the speaker, who asks her to show more regard for his eyes.

l: Naso, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The speaker complains that he has suffered for his mistress’s perjury even though the Gods have witnessed her oaths. He questions the Gods’ justice and says that, if he were a Divinity, he would allow a beautiful woman to swear falsely with impunity.

l: the Gods, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The Gods are accused of allowing beautiful women to commit perjury without punishment and of favoring the charming fair. They punish or have punished others with divine weapons and flames, but they fear to hurt the fair.

l: beauty, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: Beauty is presented as having divine sway over the Gods. The mistress’s beauty remains unchanged after her perjury, and her beauty is treated as a reason for the Gods’ excessive leniency.

l: perjuries (mistress's false oaths), The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The mistress’s perjury consists of breaking oaths sworn to the Gods and to the speaker. The speaker says that her perjuries go unpunished, although others have suffered for their offenses.

l: punishment, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY III.
s: The speaker suffers punishment for the mistress’s wrongdoing and asks whether he is to be the victim of the deceiver. The text contrasts his suffering and the mistress’s impunity with the punishments of Semele and others struck by divine power.

l: The Amores, or Amours, The Amores, or Amours, ELEGY IV.
s: The speaker advises a jealous husband that guarding his wife cannot make her chaste, because chastity must come from her own feelings and choice. Excessive surveillance and restraint instead increase temptation by making forbidden things more desirable. He cites Danaë, Penelope, and other examples to show that confinement does not prevent desire or wrongdoing. He urges the husband to treat his wife with indulgence and courtesy rather than asserting severe authority.
